1.cue: used by routers to forward a data packet
1.tip: Routers think in IP: they read WHERE the packet is going, the destination IP address. MAC addresses change at every hop.
1.why: A router looks up the destination IP address in its routing table to pick the next hop. Data-link (MAC) addresses only matter on one link and are rewritten by every router.

2.cue: destination host in the same LAN
2.tip: Same LAN = straight there. The gateway is only for leaving the LAN.
2.why: When the destination is on your own network, your PC uses ARP to learn its MAC address and sends the frame straight to it. The default gateway is only used for other networks.

3.cue: packet needs to be forwarded out the Gigabit 0/1
3.tip: Router steps: strip old frame, look up route, build a NEW frame for the exit link.
3.why: The router already chose the exit interface, so the routing lookup is done. Next it wraps the packet in a new Layer 2 frame with new MAC addresses for the next link.

4.tip: 127.0.0.1 = "there's no place like home". 127.0.0.0 is the network, not a host.
4.why: The 127.0.0.0/8 block is reserved for loopback, and 127.0.0.1 is the usual host address you ping to test your own TCP/IP stack. 127.0.0.0 is the network address, not a usable host.

5.cue: cannot access devices on other networks
5.tip: Local works, remote fails = check the default gateway, your door out of the LAN.
5.why: Reaching local devices proves the cable, IP address and mask are fine. Traffic to other networks goes through the default gateway, so a wrong gateway breaks only remote access.

6.tip: IP is "best effort": it doesn't fix lost or out-of-order packets. TCP, up above, does that.
6.why: IP is connectionless and unreliable on purpose. It just delivers packets as best it can, and upper layers like TCP handle missing or out-of-order data.

7.tip: NAT exists because IPv4 ran out of addresses. IPv6 has so many that everyone gets a public one.
7.why: NAT was created to share a few public IPv4 addresses among many hosts. IPv6 has a huge address space, so every device can have its own public address and NAT isn't needed.

8.tip: Metric is like golf: the LOWER score wins.
8.why: A metric is the cost of a route, such as hop count or bandwidth. When there are several routes to the same network, the router picks the one with the lowest metric.

9.cue: services provided by the OSI network layer

keys.k: encapsulating PDUs from the transport layer

9.tip: Layer 3 = route and wrap: it wraps segments into packets and routes them. Frames and collisions are Layer 2.
9.why: The network layer takes segments from the transport layer, adds an IP header to make packets, and routes them toward the destination. Placing frames on media and collision detection belong to Layer 2.

10.cue: switch with a default gateway address
10.tip: The switch gateway is for the switch's OWN traffic, like replies to a remote admin. Hosts use their own gateway.
10.why: A Layer 2 switch only needs a gateway for packets it creates itself, such as SSH replies to a manager on another network. Traffic from hosts passing through the switch doesn't use it.

11.cue: basic characteristic of the IP protocol
11.tip: IP: no handshake, no setup. Just send. Connectionless.
11.why: IP doesn't set up a connection before sending packets and doesn't track them. It's connectionless, media independent and best effort, so reliability is left to TCP.

12.cue: prevent a packet from traversing a network endlessly
12.tip: TTL counts down by 1 at every router. At 0 the packet dies, so loops can't last forever.
12.why: Each router lowers the Time-to-Live value by one. When it reaches zero, the packet is dropped, which stops packets from circling forever in a routing loop.

13.tip: Fewer fields, no checksum = routers work faster. Simple header, efficient handling.
13.why: The IPv6 header has fewer fields and no header checksum, so routers process packets faster. It isn't smaller overall, since IPv6 addresses are much longer than IPv4 ones.

14.tip: Which protocol is inside? Look at the Protocol field (6 = TCP, 17 = UDP).
14.why: The Protocol field tells the receiver what is carried inside the packet, like TCP, UDP or ICMP, so it can hand the data to the right upper-layer process.

15.tip: Loopback never leaves your PC, so it only tests your own TCP/IP stack.
15.why: Pinging 127.0.0.1 sends traffic back to yourself without touching the NIC or cable. If it works, the TCP/IP software on your device is working, but it says nothing about the network.

16.cue: next hop address associated with a destination network
16.tip: Remote = far away = needs a next hop. Connected (C) and local (L) routes need none.
16.why: Remote routes lead to networks that are not attached to the router, so they list a next-hop router address. Directly connected and local routes use the router's own interfaces.

17.cue: hosts ensure that their packets are directed
17.tip: Even a PC has a small routing table: loopback, local network, and a default route to the gateway.
17.why: A host keeps its own routing table. It checks if the destination is local or remote: local packets go straight out, remote packets use the default route to the gateway.

18.cue: maintain the same path for the packets
18.tip: Same conversation, same path = one FLOW. Flow Label keeps streaming packets together.
18.why: The IPv6 Flow Label marks packets that belong to the same flow, like a video stream, so routers can handle them the same way. Traffic Class is about priority, not path.

19.cue: function of the Address Resolution Protocol
19.tip: ARP: I know the IP, I need the MAC. And only on my LOCAL network.
19.why: ARP turns a known IPv4 address into a MAC address. It uses broadcasts, which routers block, so it only works on the local network.

20.cue: switch flood a frame out of every port
20.tip: Switch floods for 2 reasons: broadcast, or "I don't know where that MAC is" (unknown unicast).
20.why: A switch floods a frame when it's a broadcast, or when the destination MAC isn't in its table yet. Source addresses are only used for learning, never for forwarding decisions.

21.cue: treatment of ARP requests on the local link
21.tip: ARP request = broadcast = everyone opens it. Only the target answers.
21.why: An ARP request is sent to the broadcast MAC address, so every device on the LAN receives and processes it. Only the device with the matching IP address sends a reply.

22.cue: destination address is used in an ARP request
22.tip: All F's = all devices. 255.255.255.255 is an IP broadcast, but frames need a MAC.
22.why: An ARP request is a Layer 2 broadcast, so its destination MAC is all ones: FFFF.FFFF.FFFF. The IP broadcast 255.255.255.255 is a Layer 3 address, not a frame address.

23.why: The arp -d * command deletes all entries in the PC's ARP cache. The PC then learns fresh MAC addresses, which helps after a router change. To view the cache you'd use arp -a.

24.cue: PC1 has sent a frame addressed to PC3
24.tip: PC3's MAC isn't in the table = unknown unicast = flood out every port except where it came in.
24.why: The table only has ports 1 and 3, so PC3's MAC is unknown. The switch floods the frame out every port except port 4, where PC1's frame came in.

25.cue: IPv6 messages are used in place of ARP
25.tip: IPv6 ND: Solicitation asks ("who has?"), Advertisement answers ("me!").
25.why: IPv6 has no ARP. It uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Discovery: a Neighbor Solicitation asks for a MAC address, and a Neighbor Advertisement replies with it.

26.cue: aim of an ARP spoofing attack
26.tip: Spoofing = lying. The attacker lies about which MAC owns an IP, so traffic goes to them.
26.why: In ARP spoofing, the attacker sends fake ARP replies so an IP address, often the gateway's, maps to the attacker's MAC. Then traffic meant for that IP goes to the attacker.

27.cue: PC1 attempts to connect to File_server1
27.tip: Server on another network? ARP for the GATEWAY, not the server.
27.why: File_server1 is on a different network, so PC1 sends the frame to its default gateway. It ARPs for the gateway, so the reply holds the MAC of R1's G0/0, the LAN-side router port.

28.cue: IPv4 address to Layer 2 Ethernet address mappings
28.tip: IP-to-MAC on a host = ARP cache. MAC-to-port on a switch = MAC address table.
28.why: A host saves the IPv4-to-MAC results it learns through ARP in its ARP cache. The MAC address table is on switches, and the neighbor table is used for IPv6.

29.cue: examined in the Ethernet frame header by a Layer 2 device
29.tip: Switches forward by DESTINATION MAC. They learn from the source MAC.
29.why: A switch looks at the destination MAC address to decide which port to send the frame out. It uses the source MAC only to learn, and it never reads IP addresses.

30.cue: test whether the banner is properly configured
30.tip: Banner shows at login. Log out of privileged EXEC, press Enter, and see it. No reboot needed.
30.why: The MOTD banner appears when you start a new session. Exiting privileged EXEC mode and pressing Enter brings back the login screen, showing the banner right away without rebooting.

keys.k: retain contents when power is removed

31.tip: NV = Non-Volatile: it keeps data with no power. That's where the startup-config lives.
31.why: NVRAM is non-volatile, so it keeps its data when the power is off, and the router stores the startup configuration there. The running config, routing table and ARP table live in RAM.

32.cue: router boots and enters setup mode
32.tip: No startup-config in NVRAM = nothing to load = setup mode asks you questions.
32.why: After loading IOS, the router looks for the startup configuration in NVRAM. If there is none, it starts setup mode, a question-based wizard for a basic config.

33.tip: Switch gateway = a way home for its replies. Without it, you can only manage it from the same subnet.
33.why: A Layer 2 switch needs a default gateway to send replies to other networks. With it set, an admin on a different network can reach the switch with SSH or Telnet.

34.tip: SSH = Secure SHell. "transport input ssh" lets only encrypted logins in, no Telnet.
34.why: This command allows only SSH on the vty lines, so remote sessions are encrypted. Telnet, which sends everything in plain text, is blocked.

35.cue: forward its data off the local network
35.tip: In tracert, hop 1 is your default gateway.
35.why: The first hop in the tracert output is the first router the PC reaches, which is its default gateway: 172.20.0.254. The PC sends all off-network traffic there.

36.cue: secure access to a router through a connection to the console
36.tip: Console = line console 0, then password, then login. vty lines are for remote access.
36.why: You enter console line mode with line console 0, set the password with password cisco, and make the router ask for it with login. line vty 0 4 is for Telnet and SSH.

37.cue: description of the default gateway address

keys.k: connects the PC1 LAN to Router1

37.tip: Default gateway = the router port on YOUR LAN, the door out of your network.
37.why: A host's default gateway is the router interface on the host's own LAN. PC1 sends remote traffic to that interface. The switch isn't a gateway and the Internet-side port isn't on PC1's LAN.

38.tip: Router's 2 jobs: pick the path, then forward the packet.
38.why: A router chooses the best path to a destination using its routing table, then forwards the packet out the right interface. Microsegmentation is a switch job, and name resolution is DNS.

39.tip: Running config lives in RAM. Saving it copies to startup-config in NVRAM.
39.why: This command saves the active configuration from RAM into the startup configuration, which is stored in NVRAM. So the NVRAM contents change and the config survives a reboot.

40.cue: default gateway address is incorrectly configured
40.tip: Wrong gateway = stuck at home. Local works, remote fails.
40.why: The default gateway is only used for traffic leaving the local network. With a wrong gateway, the host still talks to local devices but can't reach hosts on other networks.

41.cue: network problems that can result from ARP operation
41.tip: ARP problems: Broadcasts slow things down, and Bad guys spoof replies. 2 B's.
41.why: ARP requests are broadcasts, so many of them can slow a busy, low-bandwidth network. ARP also trusts any reply, so an attacker can fake mappings to intercept traffic.

42.tip: Next level protocol inside = the Protocol field. Name says it.
42.why: The Protocol field holds a number that tells which upper-layer protocol is inside the packet, like 6 for TCP or 17 for UDP, so the receiver passes it to the right place.

43.cue: 8-bit binary value used to determine the priority
43.tip: Priority = treat packets DIFFERENTLY. Differentiated Services (DS) is for QoS.
43.why: The 8-bit Differentiated Services field marks how important a packet is, so devices using QoS can give priority to things like voice traffic.

44.cue: 32-bit binary value associated with an interface on the sending device
44.tip: Sending device = SOURCE. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits.
44.why: The source IPv4 address is the 32-bit address of the interface that sent the packet. The receiver uses it to know where to send a reply.

45.cue: detect corruption in the IPv4 header
45.tip: Checksum = check for damage. It only covers the header.
45.why: The header checksum is a value computed over the IPv4 header. Each router recalculates it, and if it doesn't match, the header is corrupted and the packet is dropped.

46.cue: contains a unicast, multicast, or broadcast address
46.tip: Who gets it? One, a group, or all: that's the destination's job. A source is always unicast.
46.why: The destination IPv4 address can be unicast (one host), multicast (a group) or broadcast (all hosts). The source address is always a single host, so it is always unicast.

47.cue: limit the lifetime of a packet
47.tip: TTL = Time To Live = a packet's lifetime.
47.why: Time to Live starts at a number and each router subtracts one. When it reaches zero, the packet is dropped, so it can't live forever in the network.

48.tip: 0100 in binary = 4 = IPv4. The Version field.
48.why: The first field of every IP header is the 4-bit Version field. In IPv4 it is 0100, which is 4 in decimal. In IPv6 it would be 0110, which is 6.

49.tip: Next level protocol inside = the Protocol field. Name says it.
49.why: The Protocol field holds a number that tells which upper-layer protocol is inside the packet, like 6 for TCP or 17 for UDP, so the receiver passes it to the right place.

50.tip: 0100 in binary = 4 = IPv4. The Version field.
50.why: The first field of every IP header is the 4-bit Version field. In IPv4 it is 0100, which is 4 in decimal. In IPv6 it would be 0110, which is 6.

51.tip: ARP entries have a timer. They stay until the timeout expires, then get purged.
51.why: Each ARP cache entry is time-stamped. It stays in memory until its timeout runs out, so the host doesn't have to ARP again for every packet. Then old entries are removed.

52.cue: MAC addresses of frequently used servers to be fixed
52.tip: Fixed = static. You type it in by hand, and it doesn't time out.
52.why: You can add a static ARP entry by hand that maps an IP address to a MAC address. Static entries don't expire, so a busy server's MAC stays fixed in the table.

53.cue: MAC addresses of frequently used servers to be fixed
53.tip: Fixed = static. You type it in by hand, and it doesn't time out.
53.why: You can add a static ARP entry by hand that maps an IP address to a MAC address. Static entries don't expire, so a busy server's MAC stays fixed in the table.

54.tip: To reach far away, you first need the gateway's MAC. ARP finds it.
54.why: For a remote destination, the host frames the packet to its default gateway. ARP lets the host learn the gateway's MAC address so it can build that frame.

55.cue: forces all Ethernet NICs to process an ARP request
55.tip: All F's = broadcast = every NIC has to look at it.
55.why: The ARP request's destination MAC is the broadcast address FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF. Every NIC accepts broadcast frames, so all of them process the request.

56.cue: reply only to the source sending an ARP request
56.tip: Reply goes back to the sender. The request carries the SOURCE MAC, so the target knows where to send it.
56.why: The ARP request contains the sender's source MAC address. The target uses it to send a unicast reply straight back to that one host, not a broadcast.

57.cue: flooded out all ports of a switch
57.tip: Broadcast MAC (all F's) = switch floods it everywhere except the port it came in on.
57.why: A switch floods any frame sent to the broadcast MAC FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF out every port except the one it arrived on. The ARP request uses this address.

58.cue: pass the data portion of the Ethernet frame to the ARP process
58.tip: EtherType tells who gets the payload: 0x806 = ARP, 0x800 = IPv4.
58.why: The EtherType field in the frame header says what's inside. The value 0x806 tells the NIC that the payload is ARP, so the data is handed to the ARP process.

59.cue: pass the data portion of the Ethernet frame to the ARP process
59.tip: EtherType tells who gets the payload: 0x806 = ARP, 0x800 = IPv4.
59.why: The EtherType field in the frame header says what's inside. The value 0x806 tells the NIC that the payload is ARP, so the data is handed to the ARP process.

60.cue: Match the packets with their destination IP address to the exiting
60.tip: Match the 3rd number to a route: .6 Fa0/0, .10 Fa1/1, .12 Fa1/0, .14 Fa0/1. No route (.8)? Default route, Serial0/0/0.
60.why: The router matches each destination to its 172.17.x.0/24 route and uses that exit port. 172.17.8.0 is not in the table, so that packet follows the default route out Serial0/0/0.

61.cue: Match the commands to the correct actions
61.tip: config-line password = console security. hostname = name. banner motd = message of the day.
61.why: A password set in line config mode protects that line, like the console. hostname gives the router a name, and banner motd sets a message shown when someone connects.

62.cue: manage routers and switches locally and remotely

keys.k: SSH remote access method that uses encryption
AUX remote access via a dialup

62.tip: Telnet = plain text. SSH = encrypted. AUX = modem dial-up. Console = cable plugged in locally.
62.why: Telnet sends everything in clear text, so it's unsecure. SSH encrypts the session. The AUX port connects to a modem for dial-up. The console port is the main out-of-band method.

63.cue: phases to the functions during the boot up process

keys.k: POST and load the bootstrap program phase 1

63.tip: Boot order: Test, IOS, Config. Hardware first, then the OS, then your settings.
63.why: First the router tests its hardware (POST) and loads the bootstrap. Then it finds and loads IOS. Last, it loads the startup configuration from NVRAM.

64.cue: Match the command with the device mode
64.tip: > user, # privileged, (config) global, (config-if) interface, (config-line) line. Match each command to what it changes.
64.why: enable runs from user mode (>), and saving the config needs privileged EXEC (#). service password-encryption is global, login is a line setting, and an IP address goes on an interface.

65.cue: Match the configuration mode with the command that is available
65.tip: Climb the ladder: > (enable) to # (copy) to (config) (interface) and (config-line) (login).
65.why: enable is typed at the user prompt R1>. copy running-config needs privileged R1#. You enter an interface from global config, and login is set inside line config mode.
